title: Sources, essays, historiography and the IA
summary: How to evaluate sources with origin, purpose and content, how to compare sources, how to plan an argued essay, how to use historiography, and how the historical investigation is structured.

keyterms.definition: Evidence produced at or close to the time studied, such as a letter, speech, photograph or cartoon.
A later interpretation of the past produced by someone using evidence, such as a historian's book.
Who produced a source, when, where and in what form; used to judge its value and limitations.
Why a source was created and for whom, which affects what it includes and leaves out.
How useful a source is to a historian for a given enquiry, and what restricts that usefulness.
Checking a source against other evidence to see whether it is supported.
The study of how historians have interpreted a topic and why their interpretations differ.
The clear, arguable answer to an essay question, stated in the introduction and sustained throughout.
The instruction word in a question, such as 'evaluate', 'compare and contrast' or 'to what extent'.
The IA: a 2,200-word investigation with three sections, source evaluation, investigation and reflection.

questions.prompt: In a value and limitations question, which is the strongest comment on origin?
options: It was written by a Soviet minister in 1947, so it is valuable for revealing the official Soviet view at the start of the Cold War
It is a primary source, so it is reliable
It is old, so it is biased
It is written in English
questions.explanation: Strong answers explain how the specific origin affects the source's value for a historian, rather than giving generic labels.

questions.statement: A biased source can still be valuable to a historian.
questions.explanation: Propaganda is valuable evidence of what a regime wanted people to believe and how it sought to persuade them.

questions.text: Why a source was created and for whom is its ___.
questions.explanation: A speech to party members may differ from a private letter on the same subject because the purposes differ.

questions.prompt: Match each Paper 1 question type to its demand.

pairs.right: Show understanding of a source's content or message
Analyse value and limitations using origin, purpose, content
Use sources and own knowledge to answer a question

questions.explanation: Paper 1 has four questions worth 24 marks in one hour.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to structure a compare-and-contrast answer?
options: Run linked comparisons point by point, using phrases like 'both' and 'whereas'
Describe Source A fully and then Source B fully
Only discuss similarities
Discuss the authors' biographies
questions.explanation: Examiners reward explicit, linked comparisons; separate descriptions ('end-on' answers) score poorly.

questions.statement: In the final Paper 1 question, using only the sources without own knowledge can reach the top markband.
questions.explanation: The top band requires the sources and accurate own knowledge to be integrated in a focused argument.

questions.text: A historian's book written in 2010 about the 1930s is a ___ source.
questions.explanation: Its value often lies in hindsight and access to a range of evidence, including archives.

questions.prompt: Which is a genuine limitation of a memoir written 30 years after the events?
options: The author may misremember or justify their past actions with hindsight
It cannot contain any facts
It is automatically less valuable than any newspaper
It was written in the past
questions.explanation: Limitations should be specific: self-justification and memory are real problems with memoirs.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of analysing a political cartoon in a sensible order.
items: Identify the cartoonist, publication and date
Explain the message in its historical context
questions.explanation: Context and provenance come first, then interpretation, then evaluation.

options: Checking a source against other evidence
Copying a source's wording
Rejecting any biased source
Finding the author's birthday
questions.explanation: Cross-referencing sources helps establish how far a claim can be trusted.

lessons.title: Essays, historiography and the historical investigation

questions.prompt: What should the introduction of a Paper 2 essay contain?
options: A clear thesis answering the question and an outline of the argument
A long narrative of background events
Quotations from as many historians as possible
A summary of the conclusion of every paragraph in detail
questions.explanation: A focused thesis shows the examiner from the start that you understand the demands of the question.

questions.text: Each Paper 2 and Paper 3 essay is marked out of ___.
questions.explanation: Essays are marked with level descriptors; the top band rewards focused, well-supported, evaluative arguments.

questions.statement: A question that asks you to discuss 'two countries from different regions' requires examples from two of the IB's four regions.
questions.explanation: Paper 2 questions often specify regions; ignoring the requirement limits marks.

questions.prompt: Match each command term to what it requires.

pairs.right: Weigh the merits of an argument and judge

questions.explanation: Responding to the command term is central to staying focused.

questions.prompt: How should historiography be used in an essay?
options: To support or challenge your own argument, with your own judgement on the evidence
As a list of historians' names in the conclusion
Instead of factual evidence
Only in the introduction
questions.explanation: Historiography is not required for the top band, but used well it shows awareness of different perspectives.

questions.prompt: Put the sections of the historical investigation in order.
questions.explanation: Sections 1–3 are assessed by criteria A–C; the bibliography is required but not part of the word count.

questions.text: The historical investigation has a limit of ___ words.
questions.explanation: Exceeding the limit means the examiner stops reading, which can cost marks for the conclusion and reflection.

questions.statement: Criterion B (Investigation) is worth the most marks in the IA.
questions.explanation: Criterion B is worth 15 of the 25 marks; A is worth 6 and C is worth 4.

questions.prompt: What should the IA reflection section focus on?
options: What the investigation revealed about the methods and challenges historians face
A summary of the findings
How much the student enjoyed the topic
A list of further reading
questions.explanation: Good reflection links issues such as selection, bias or the nature of evidence to the student's own investigation.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph opening is most analytical?
options: The most important reason Stalin won the power struggle was his control of the party apparatus as General Secretary.
In 1922 Stalin became General Secretary.
Stalin was born in Georgia in 1878.
There were many events in the 1920s.
questions.explanation: An analytical topic sentence makes a claim linked to the question, which the paragraph then supports with evidence.
